doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York clubs and the Embers trio
title: Club pay in the early 1950s: scale, commissions and free coffee
summary: A trio at the Hickory House earned about $550 to $600 a week between three people, minus agent commission and union dues, and the owner John Popkin complained about free coffee.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah, speaking of rent, that gives me an idea for another question, is that, maybe you can tell our listeners what the average pay per week for musicians, sideman and a leader, say at Embers or Storyville or some of the clubs, what that would average. Would it be a little different on the road as opposed to being in New York, I would think?
Yeah, it was different, but it was awfully low, and I . . . when I think of how little . . . I can only pinpoint the Hickory House. I think it was something like $550 or $600, between three people.
We realize that we’re talking about over 40 years ago too.
Yeah, but that was considered not too bad.
For that time it probably wasn’t too bad.
And then give a commission out of that, too.
Oh the agents were collecting commissions?
Pretty awful, isn’t it? And then union dues.
And then all we got from the club would be cups of coffee. John Popkin would say, “I’m sick of keeping you people in free coffee.” He’d get mad if he lost at the racetrack.
He didn’t serve meals to you?
Not free. You got a discount. You could eat anything you wanted.
